refs.q: a little river ran through it, from which went narrow leats held up by hatches, so that the more part of the valley bottom was a water-meadow

refs.q: She was very tall, a full half-head taller than any of her women

facts.subject: Wall of the World
facts.statement: Otter says no living person of these parts has seen the true Wall of the World; the name may mean something else.

refs.q: this word is at whiles said of something else, which no man alive amongst us has yet seen

facts.statement: Old men say it is a toy, an image of the real Dry Tree near the Well.

refs.q: it is but a toy, and an image of that which is verily anigh the Well at the World's End

facts.subject: Well at the World's End
facts.statement: Seekers from Utterbol's land never returned.

refs.q: they never came back again to us

facts.subject: Lord of Utterbol
facts.statement: Free men count for little; useful thralls rule.

refs.q: in my Lord's land the free men are of little account, since they must oftenest do as my Lord and my Lord's thralls bid them

facts.subject: Dale of the Tower

facts.subject: Lord of Utterbol

refs.q: I have cheapened a likely thrall of Morfinn the Unmanned, and he is a gift to thee

refs.q: a place where is naught but a ledge, and then below it a gulf filled with nothing but the howling of winds

basis_refs.q: an image of that which is verily anigh the Well

ledger.summary: At dawn Ralph sees the mountains in the east as a huge black wall, ranges rising one behind another, still far off. Otter muses that beyond may be a plain, endless mountains, or the world's edge over a howling gulf, and that the mountains make the local folk harsh, "thralls of the great mountains". He says "Wall of the World" may also mean something else no living man has seen; a much-worshipped Dry Tree stands not far from Utterbol on the hither side, said to be only an image of the true one near the Well; seekers from here never came back. Two hours before noon they reach the Dale of the Tower: a shallow dale with a river channelled into water-meadows by leats and hatches, a grange among elms, cots, and a great square tower on a mound flying the Lord's banner. The Lady of Utterbol's white, gold and purple pavilion is there. Otter says he was once a thrall and that in Utterbol the clever thralls rise above free men. The Lady is very tall with yellow hair and blue eyes; her women are barefoot thralls with iron arm-rings. When the Lord offers Ralph to her as a gift, she blushes and looks down at the sight of him.
ledger.geography_notes: The mountains lie east, dark blue and huge, one range behind another, far away. The Dale of the Tower: over a long down, a shallow, well-grassed dale; a little river with leats and hatches feeding water-meadows; willows; a grange with many roofs among tall elms in a bend of the river; two or three cots on the near slope and about six by the grange; a great square tower with barriers and bailey on a mound away from the river and grange; a causeway above the meadows.
